companies.companies/0/profile/about:
The company installs ventilated rainscreen façades on public and residential buildings and supplies aluminium subsystems of its own assembly. We work to the client's design or to our own shop drawings: junction details, wind-load calculations, colour approvals with the architect.

We take on buildings from 2,000 m² of façade. Concealed work is checked stage by stage: brackets, insulation, wind barrier, rails, cladding. Each stage closes with a photo-documented report that the client can open in the project on the platform.

We buy metal and fixings directly from manufacturers, so we act as buyer and seller at the same time: this is visible in our requests for quotation and in the catalogue.

events.events/0/body:
The main industry meeting of the year on façades. Three days, thirty sessions, a place where designers, contractors, manufacturers and supervision talk to each other.

## Who it is for

Project and site managers, procurement specialists, production technologists, façade designers and technical supervision specialists.

## What is on

- A walk through the new fire-test requirements for cladding with representatives of testing centres.
- Practice of staged acceptance of concealed layers: reports, photo records, disputes.
- Manufacturers' session: product passports, batch test reports, delivery times.
- Contractors' open microphone: typical installation mistakes and how to avoid them.

## Format

In-person participation with access to all sessions and stands, or online participation with a stream of the business programme. Session recordings stay available to participants for a week after the event.

publications.publications/0/lede: The updated standard clarifies requirements for fixings and testing; manufacturers will get a transition period.
publications.publications/0/versions/0/title: New ventilated façade standard comes into force in spring
publications.publications/0/versions/1/body:
An industry publication reports that the updated standard for ventilated rainscreen façade systems comes into force on 1 March. The first version of this note gave a wrong date, 1 February; the editors corrected the error after checking with the authors of the document. The standard replaces the edition in force since 2019 and concerns designers, subsystem manufacturers and installation companies.

## What changes

The main changes concern fixings and testing. The document tightens the requirements for anchors and brackets: every type of substrate now needs a pull-out test report, performed on site or on a sample of the same material. Wind-load tests follow an updated scheme that takes the gust component into account for buildings taller than 75 metres.

- The product passport must state the design load capacity of the bracket for every type of substrate.
- For cladding heavier than 40 kilograms per square metre, a mandatory cyclic-load check of the fixing detail is introduced.
- The installation company records anchor tightening torques in the site log, not only in the concealed-works report.

## Transition period

Subsystem manufacturers receive a six-month transition period to update product passports. Projects that passed review before the standard takes effect may be completed under the previous requirements, but the client may demand that details be checked by the new method at acceptance.

> "For conscientious manufacturers the new standard changes nothing fundamental: we tested fixings on every type of substrate anyway. The difference is that it is now an obligation, not an argument in a dispute," notes the technical director of a subsystem manufacturer.

## What it means for the market

Designers should request updated passports from suppliers in advance: without them, fixing-detail calculations will not pass review after March. Installation companies will have to revise the site log form and train crews to record tightening torques. For clients the new standard offers a clearer acceptance tool: test reports become part of the as-built documentation.

## What comes next

The authors of the standard promise to publish methodological guidance on testing within a month. The editors are following the updates and will prepare a review with worked calculations once the guidance is out.

publications.publications/1/versions/0/body:
A thermal insulation manufacturer has announced the launch of a new mineral wool board line at its site in the Bukhara region. According to the press office, the line's capacity is 1.2 million cubic metres a year, and the first shipments are planned for November. The editors quote the company's figures without independent verification of volumes.

## What was launched

The line produces boards with densities from 35 to 180 kilograms per cubic metre for façade, roofing and render systems. The manufacturer states that the equipment can change density without stopping the line, and that automatic geometry control reduces the share of rejects.

- Thickness range: 50 to 200 millimetres.
- Boards for ventilated façades are supplied faced with glass fleece.
- Packaging carries a batch code that can be used to request the test report.

## Why the market needs it

Demand for non-combustible insulation in the region is growing faster than supply: market participants estimate that a significant share of the volume is still brought in from distant regions, which adds logistics to the price and two or three weeks to the lead time. Local production should shorten the delivery leg for sites in Bukhara, Navoi and Samarkand.

> "What matters to a contractor is not record capacity figures but predictability: that a batch arrives on time and matches the previous one in properties. If the plant ensures that, it will be accepted quickly," says the head of procurement at an installation company.

## What to watch

The editors recommend requesting test reports for the first batches from the new manufacturer and comparing the declared properties with the design values. The batch quality passport must state thermal conductivity, compressive strength and water absorption at partial immersion.

## What comes next

The company plans to certify its products for use in external thermal insulation composite systems with a thin render layer by the end of the year. The editors have asked the manufacturer for samples for independent testing and will publish the results when they are ready.

publications.publications/2/lede: Model exchange, level of development and model-based acceptance: three topics contractors kept returning to.
publications.publications/2/versions/0/body:
A two-day conference on information modelling in construction has ended in Tashkent. The editors picked out three topics that contractors kept returning to: exchanging models between participants, the required level of detail, and acceptance of work against the model.

## Exchanging models

Most of the contractors who spoke face the same problem: the designer delivers the model in one format, the client requires reporting in another, and subcontractors work in a third. Losses in conversion lead to discrepancies in quantities and disputes when closing acceptance reports.

- Participants propose fixing the exchange format and the list of attributes in the contract, not in correspondence.
- Several companies showed procedures in which a designated coordinator on the client's side is responsible for the integrity of the model.
- A separate discussion unfolded around change history: who made an edit and when should be visible without a request to the designer.

## Level of detail

The second topic is a mismatch of expectations. Clients expect the model to be accurate enough to procure materials, while designers plan a level sufficient to approve design decisions. The gap is closed either by additional work on the contractor's side or by errors in the order.

> "We spent three weeks bringing the model to a level at which the façade subsystem could be quantified. It was not paid for, because the contract said nothing about it," said a project manager at an installation company.

## Acceptance against the model

The third topic is acceptance. Several clients described the practice of comparing the as-built survey with the model: deviations are recorded automatically, and the report is produced from the comparison. Contractors are cautious about the approach: tolerances in the model are often stricter than in the standards, and this becomes a source of penalties.

## What comes next

The organisers promised to publish session recordings and a digest of participants' proposals. The editors prepared this note with the help of the assistant from the conference materials; the text was checked by an editor. A review of standard contract clauses for model exchange will follow as a separate piece.

publications.publications/3/lede: Cyclic tests and the authors' caveat: the conclusions apply only to the samples studied.
publications.publications/3/versions/0/body:
A scientific journal has published the results of a study on the durability of clinker tiles in a frosty climate. The authors ran cyclic tests on samples from five manufacturers and compared the results with survey data from façades that had been in service for five to twelve years in the Namangan region.

## How the tests were run

Samples were subjected to 150 freeze-thaw cycles in a water-saturated state, after which mass loss, flexural strength and the condition of the face were measured. In parallel, six buildings with clinker cladding were surveyed and their defects compared with the laboratory results.

- Samples with water absorption below three percent passed the tests without visible defects.
- In samples with water absorption above six percent, flaking of the face layer began after 90 cycles.
- On the buildings, defects were concentrated in zones with poor drainage: under sills, at parapets and at the plinth.

## The authors' caveats

The authors stress that the conclusions apply only to the samples studied and cannot be transferred to the manufacturers' whole product range. The condition of the façades depended less on the tile than on the quality of the joint grout and the drainage details.

> "The strongest tile will not save a façade if water sits in the joint. The study confirms with numbers what used to be only the experience of site foremen," comments one of the authors.

## What it means in practice

Designers should specify not only the frost-resistance grade but also the maximum water absorption. Installers should pay attention to joint sealing and sill slopes. Clients should demand test reports for the specific batch, not catalogue data.

## What comes next

The authors plan to continue monitoring the surveyed buildings and publish data in three years. The editors will add the study to the collection on choosing cladding for a cold climate.

publications.publications/4/quiz/0/question: Why can two façade panel proposals not be compared by a single figure?
publications.publications/4/versions/0/body:
Two commercial proposals for façade panels can almost never be compared head-on: different units of measurement, different quantities behind the calculation and unnoticed material substitutions make the price per square metre meaningless. We examine three causes of discrepancies and suggest a simple order of checks.

## Units of measurement

One supplier counts in square metres of cladding, another in panels, a third in linear metres of subsystem. All of this is legitimate, but to compare you must bring the proposals to one base. The most reliable way is to ask for a calculation on a specific façade fragment with a drawing, not on an "average building".

- Request a calculation on the same fragment with the same openings and corners.
- Clarify whether offcuts and the cutting allowance are included in the price: usually five to twelve percent.
- Check that fixings and trim pieces are counted in the same units as the panels.

## Quantities

The quantity in a proposal is often taken from the design at the approval stage, where the façade is not yet detailed. The difference from the shop drawings reaches fifteen percent, and a cheap proposal becomes expensive once quantities are refined. Ask the supplier to record which documentation the calculation is based on and how the price will be recalculated if the quantity changes.

> "We stopped comparing proposals by the total. We compare unit rates on a fragment and the recalculation terms; that shows who prices the risk in and who puts it in an addendum," says the head of purchasing at an installation company.

## Substitutions

The most insidious cause is a change of material without a change of name in the specification. A panel of the same thickness may have a different reaction-to-fire class, a different density or a different coating. Ask for product passports and test reports for the specific batch, not catalogue sheets.

## Order of checks

Units first, then quantities, then substitutions. If a proposal fails the first step, the second and third no longer matter. The supplier request checklist published in the "Handy references" section helps ask all the questions in advance.

publications.publications/5/lede: A project manager's personal experience: how stage acceptance removes disputes at the end of a project.
publications.publications/5/versions/0/body:
Accepting a façade at the end of a project turns every comment into a dispute: the contractor has already struck the scaffolding, subcontractors have left, and the client sees the result for the first time. I describe how we moved to staged acceptance and what it changed.

## Why acceptance at the end does not work

A façade system hides four layers: fixings, insulation, wind barrier and cladding. Once the cladding is installed, the first three cannot be checked without dismantling. So "end of job" reports record only what is visible and leave the client with doubts and the contractor with the risk of claims a year later.

## What we record at each stage

- Fixings: anchor pull-out test report and tightening torques from the log.
- Insulation: photo records of joints and abutments before the wind barrier goes on.
- Wind barrier: laps and taping, especially around openings.
- Cladding: joint geometry, flatness and edge condition on sample bays.

Each stage closes with a short report with photographs and a reference to the design requirement. The contractor's statement and the client's confirmation are separate records: we do not mix "done" and "checked".

> "Staged acceptance added a couple of hours a week of paperwork but removed weeks of disputes at the end. The client comes to site more often and sees what is happening under the cladding," shares a site foreman.

## What it gave us

On the last three buildings the final report was signed without comments on concealed work: every question had been settled along the way. The client received a complete set of photographs by bay, and we got arguments in case of claims.

## What I advise colleagues

Agree on staged acceptance before work starts and build it into the schedule. Better to agree the report form in advance so as not to argue about wording on site.

publications.publications/6/lede: A process engineer on which lines of a report to read first and what is most often confused.
publications.publications/6/versions/0/body:
An insulation test report is the document most often skimmed. A production process engineer explains which lines really matter and what is confused most often when checking.

## Which lines to read first

First, the test method and the date of sampling. If samples were taken from a showroom rather than from the batch, the report speaks about the product in general, not about what will arrive on site. Second, the conditioning conditions: thermal conductivity is measured at different temperatures, and the figures are not comparable without this line.

- Thermal conductivity at 10 and at 25 degrees are different values; the design uses the design value under service conditions.
- Compressive strength at ten percent deformation matters for render systems and hardly matters for ventilated façades.
- Water absorption at partial immersion shows how the material behaves in a humid climate.

## What is confused most often

Most often, the declared value and the measured value. The catalogue gives the declared value; the report gives the value measured on specific samples. The difference is acceptable within the method's error, but if the report is systematically better than the catalogue, it is worth asking why.

> "A good report is boring: there are no records in it. If everything in the report is ten percent better than the catalogue, I would ask to repeat the tests in my presence," says the technologist.

## How to request it properly

Ask for a report for the batch with its number and date, not a "typical" one. Check whether the laboratory is accredited for the method in question. Compare the density in the report with the density in the batch passport: a discrepancy means the report refers to a different product.

## What comes next

The editors are preparing a guide to reading test reports with example lines. The technologist has agreed to check the draft.

publications.publications/7/lede: Five points without which a supplier request will not produce comparable proposals.
publications.publications/7/versions/0/body:
A supplier request that lacks five points comes back as a proposal that cannot be compared with others. We publish a checklist proven on purchases of subsystems, insulation and cladding.

## The five points

- Fragment for calculation: a drawing of a façade area with openings, corners and abutments, so that all suppliers calculate the same thing.
- Units of measurement: square metres of cladding, linear metres of subsystem, pieces of fixings; state them explicitly.
- Delivery time and place: site address, bay schedule, unloading conditions.
- Documents: product passports, batch test reports, certificates for the assembled system.
- Recalculation terms: what happens to the price when quantities and dates change.

## Why it works

A supplier who receives such a request spends less time on clarifications and submits a proposal that can be placed next to the others. The client sees who reads the request carefully and who answers with a template.

> "After we switched to a single request, the number of clarifying calls halved and proposals started arriving in one format," says a purchasing specialist.

## How to use it

Copy the points into an email, attach the fragment drawing and state the response deadline. If a supplier did not send batch reports, that is not a reason to refuse but a reason to ask before signing the specification.

## What comes next

The editors are collecting standard questions by topic: delivery times, packaging, warranties. The finished lists are published in the piece "Questions for the supplier".

publications.publications/8/versions/0/body:
Over the year the logistics of mineral wool boards in the region has changed noticeably: local warehouses have appeared, the share of direct deliveries from plants has grown, and packaging requirements have risen. The review was prepared by a supplier company from its own data and market observations.

## What has changed

A year ago most of the volume was shipped from distributors' central warehouses, with a lead time of two to three weeks. Now three manufacturers have opened regional warehouses, and large sites receive boards directly from the plant to the bay schedule.

- The average lead time for standard items fell from fourteen to five days.
- The share of direct deliveries from plants grew to roughly a third of the volume.
- Packaging requirements tightened: moisture-protected pallets became the norm.

## What it means for the site

Contractors can order insulation for the work front instead of keeping a stock on site. This reduces the risk of wetting and spoilage but requires more precise planning.

> "We stopped storing insulation on site for longer than a week. The manufacturer's warehouse is now closer than our own," notes a head of procurement.

## What to watch

Shorter lead times apply to standard densities and thicknesses. Non-standard items should still be ordered three to four weeks ahead. Check availability by item code before signing the specification.

## Caveat

The review reflects the observations of one company and is not an independent market study. The editors publish it as an industry participant's contribution with the author named.

publications.publications/13/versions/0/body:
A short conversation with a project manager about how staged acceptance changes the relationship with the client. The name and company are withheld at her request: the conversation is about the method, not about people.

## Why did you abandon a single final acceptance?

Because at the end nobody remembers who decided what in March. An interim report is the project's memory: signed, photographs attached, move on. A dispute that could have arisen six months later simply does not arise.

## What was hardest in the transition?

Persuading the contractor to photograph concealed work before closing it. For the first two months we had to remind them; then people saw that the photographs protect them too.

## How do you separate the statement and the confirmation?

The contractor's statement is their words: "done". The client's confirmation is our check on site. These are two different entries in the log, and we never merge them into one line.

## What would you advise those who are starting?

Start with three stages: frame, insulation, cladding. That is enough to remove most disputes.

> She stresses that the contractor's statement and the client's confirmation must remain separate records.

publications.publications/14/versions/0/body:
Autumn on site is the time when concrete work is still going on and night frosts have already begun. A piece from last issue on anti-freeze admixtures and covering structures.

## Watch the forecast

Fresh concrete must be covered as soon as the forecast promises night temperatures below zero. Waiting for actual frost is too late: strength is gained in the first day.

## Admixtures do not replace covering

An anti-freeze admixture lowers the freezing point of the water in the mix; covering retains the heat of hydration. They work together, not instead of each other.

## Record the temperature in the log

Write down the temperature of the mix and the air at placement: it is the only argument in a quality dispute a month later.

## Remove the covering gradually

A sharp temperature drop after removing the film causes cracks. Open structures in stages, starting from the leeward side.

> Editors' tip: print the checklist and hang it in the site cabin; it is cheaper than any dispute about cracks.

publications.publications/15/lede: We go through the key parameters to look at when comparing materials.
publications.publications/15/versions/0/body:
Choosing a material rarely comes down to price. Purpose, service conditions, compatibility with adjacent layers and the origin of the batch decide whether a façade will last its design life. We go through four questions worth asking before comparing proposals.

## Purpose and context

The same material behaves differently at the plinth and on the upper floors, on the south and the north façade, in the city and by the sea. Start with the conditions: loads, humidity, temperature swings, aggressiveness of the environment. Only then does it make sense to look at catalogues.

## Performance

- Durability: service life under the declared conditions and the tests that confirm it.
- Resistance to loads: wind, impact, cyclic.
- Ease of maintenance: can one panel be replaced without dismantling its neighbours?

## Compatibility

A façade is a system, not a set of materials. Cladding, subsystem, insulation and wind barrier are tested together, and replacing one layer can take the system outside its certificate. Check that the specific combination has been tested and described in the technical approval.

> "The most expensive mistakes are not in choosing a bad material but in combining good ones that should not sit next to each other," says an engineer at a design office.

## Origin

A batch with a clear origin means a passport, test reports and traceability to the plant. Material without documents is cheaper exactly until the first claim.

## How to apply this

Write the answers to the four questions into the specification, and suppliers' proposals become comparable. The piece "How to compare proposals" describes the next step.

publications.publications/16/lede: What delivery times depend on, how to assess them and which questions to clarify with the supplier.
publications.publications/16/versions/0/body:
The delivery time in a commercial proposal is one figure behind which stands a chain of five or six links. We look at what makes up the time, how to assess it and which questions to clarify with the supplier before signing.

## What makes up the time

- Stock availability or the production cycle: days for standard items, weeks for custom ones.
- Order completion: trim pieces and fixings often come from a different warehouse.
- Logistics: shipping window, transport, unloading on site.
- Acceptance: checking completeness and documents takes time that is rarely built into the schedule.

## How to assess it

Ask the supplier to break the time down by link. If they name one figure and cannot explain what it consists of, the time is most likely optimistic. Compare not the total times but the weakest link of each supplier.

> "A supplier who honestly talks about three weeks is more reliable than one who promises a week and is two weeks late," remarks a project manager.

## Which questions to ask

Is there a batch in stock now? What happens to the time if the quantity changes by ten percent? Who is responsible for unloading? Which documents will arrive with the goods?

## How to fix it

The time by link and the recalculation terms belong in the specification. Then a postponed delivery becomes a matter of contract, not of correspondence.

publications.publications/17/lede: How modern plants are organised and what affects the stability of quality.
publications.publications/17/versions/0/body:
The consistency of a material's quality is determined not by laboratory records but by the repeatability of production. We explain how a modern line is organised and at which stages deviations most often occur.

## Incoming inspection of raw materials

Everything starts with raw materials: their composition and moisture determine the production regime. At good plants every batch of raw material passes incoming inspection, and the results are kept together with the batch number of the finished product.

## Stability of the regime

- Temperature regime and line speed are recorded automatically.
- Deviations beyond tolerance stop the line rather than being corrected by eye.
- Changeovers between densities or thicknesses are documented.

## Outgoing inspection

A finished batch is checked for geometry, density and key performance properties. The outgoing inspection report is tied to the batch number: that is the one to request when buying.

> "Quality is not when everything is perfect in the laboratory, but when the hundredth batch does not differ from the first," says a production manager.

## Where deviations occur

Most often when raw materials change and during changeovers. So the question "which batch of raw material was my batch made from" is not idle: it shows how well the plant controls the process.

## How to use this

Request the outgoing inspection report for the batch, ask about incoming inspection of raw materials and pay attention to how the plant documents changeovers.

publications.publications/18/lede: We look at which tasks new solutions deliver real results in and how to adopt them.
publications.publications/18/versions/0/body:
New technologies in construction promise a lot but pay off only where they reduce rework, approval time or the number of disputes. We look at how to tell a real effect from a presentation.

## An effect that can be measured

A useful technology changes a measurable indicator: the percentage of rework, the approval time, the number of claims. If the team cannot name the indicator that will improve, the technology will remain a demonstration.

- A digital model pays off where people used to argue about quantities.
- Laser scanning pays off where as-built surveys took weeks.
- Electronic logs pay off where paper got lost between shifts.

## How to introduce it

Start with one site and one indicator. Do not change the whole process: add the tool where the pain is obvious and measure the result after a month.

> "We introduced scanning on one façade and saw that the as-built survey started taking a day instead of a week. After that nobody had to be persuaded," says a project manager.

## Where technology does not help

Where the problem is in the contract, not in the tool. If the client and the contractor have not agreed on tolerances, a digital model will only speed up the dispute.

## What comes next

The editors are collecting examples of measurable effects from readers. Send stories with numbers; we will publish the best.
publications.publications/19/lede: Short explanations and key terms found in specifications and proposals.
publications.publications/19/versions/0/body:
The same material properties are named differently in catalogues, test reports and specifications. A short glossary helps speak the same language as the supplier and not miss what matters in the documents.

## Thermal performance

- Thermal conductivity: the material's ability to conduct heat; the lower, the better the insulation. It is measured at a specific temperature, which must always be checked.
- Design thermal conductivity: the value for the design that accounts for service conditions, usually higher than the laboratory value.
- Thermal resistance: a property of a layer of a given thickness, not of the material in general.

## Strength

- Compressive strength at ten percent deformation: the indicator for systems where the insulation carries load.
- Delamination strength: matters for rendered façades.
- Flexural strength: a property of cladding boards and panels.

## Moisture and fire

- Water absorption at partial immersion: the material's behaviour in a humid climate.
- Vapour permeability: the ability to let water vapour through; affects the moisture regime of the wall.
- Combustibility class: a classification from non-combustible to highly combustible; façades usually require non-combustible or low-combustibility materials.

> "Half of the disputes on site arise because the parties call different things by one word. A glossary annexed to the contract solves this in a day," notes a technical supervision engineer.

## How to use it

Attach the glossary to the supplier request and ask them to use the terms exactly this way. It will make proposals comparable.
publications.publications/20/lede: Ready question lists for the important topics: deadlines, packaging, documents, warranties.
publications.publications/20/versions/0/body:
Ready-made lists of questions save time and make proposals comparable. Pick a topic, remove what you do not need and send the questions together with the request.

## Delivery times

- Is the item in stock now, and in what quantity?
- What is the production cycle for custom elements?
- What happens to the time if the quantity changes by ten percent?

## Packaging and logistics

- How is the batch packed, and is it protected from moisture?
- What transport is needed for unloading, and who provides it?
- Can the delivery be split by bays without a change in price?

## Documents

- Which documents come with the batch: passport, test reports, certificates?
- Has the system been tested as an assembly with the layers specified in the design?
- Can we get a test report for the specific batch rather than a typical one?

## Warranties

- What does the warranty cover, and what voids it?
- How is a claim filed, and within what period is it considered?
- Is there experience of deliveries to sites with similar conditions?

> "We send the same list to all suppliers. Those who answer every question usually deliver without surprises," shares a procurement specialist.

## How to use it

Copy the blocks you need into an email and ask for answers point by point. "We will clarify later" is a reason to ask again before signing.
publications.publications/21/lede: Checklists and recommendations so a meeting with a partner stays on point.
publications.publications/21/versions/0/body:
A meeting with a partner is productive when both sides have prepared for it. A short checklist helps save an hour and leave with decisions rather than impressions.

## Before the meeting

- State the goal in one sentence: what must be decided.
- Draw up a list of questions and send it in advance.
- Prepare the materials: drawings, specifications, previous proposals.
- Appoint someone responsible for the outcomes.

## At the meeting

Start with the goal and the list of questions. Record decisions as you go, not from memory afterwards. If a question cannot be settled on the spot, set a deadline and an owner.

> "We stopped holding meetings without an agenda. It is surprising how many meetings were simply cancelled after that as unnecessary," says a head of projects.

## After the meeting

Send the outcomes the same day: decisions, deadlines, owners. That is the document the parties will come back to.

## What comes next

A template for the agenda and the meeting outcomes is available in the platform's workspace.
publications.publications/22/lede: How a procurement specialist builds reliable supplies and what they pay attention to.
publications.publications/22/versions/0/body:
A procurement specialist at an installation company explains how she builds reliable supply and what she pays attention to when working with suppliers.

## Where reliability begins

With documents. I ask for passports and test reports before talking about price: if a supplier cannot provide them on request, they will not provide them at delivery either. This is the first filter, and it removes more problems than any negotiation.

## What I check in every proposal

- Units of measurement and the calculation base: one façade fragment for everyone.
- Time by link: warehouse, production, logistics, unloading.
- Recalculation terms when the quantity changes.
- The contact of the person responsible for the delivery, not for the sale.

## How I keep to schedule

I order for the work front with a week's margin and ask the supplier to confirm shipment two days ahead. If there is no confirmation, I call myself. This simple rule has saved more than one schedule.

> "A supplier who calls first when something goes wrong is worth more than any discount. We work with such suppliers for years."

## What I consider most important

Attention to detail is not pedantry but respect for the people on site who are waiting for the material. Every unchecked line in the specification turns into crew downtime.

## Advice to colleagues

Set up one request template and one proposal review template. Within a month you will see which suppliers read requests and which answer out of habit.
publications.publications/23/lede: The story of a specialist who develops a team and shares experience with younger colleagues.
publications.publications/23/versions/0/body:
A shop foreman at a subsystem plant explains how he develops his team, why mentoring matters more than instructions and what he passes on to younger colleagues.

## What the instructions leave out

The instruction says how to set up the machine. It does not say how to tell by the sound that the cutter is blunt, or why the first part after a changeover must be measured three times. That is passed on only side by side, on the shop floor.

## How mentoring is organised

- First week: the newcomer only watches and asks questions.
- Second week: works in a pair, the mentor checks every operation.
- Third week: works alone, the mentor checks the result.
- After a month: a review of mistakes without reproach, only causes and solutions.

## Why it matters to production

Consistency of quality depends on people no less than on equipment. A team in which experience is passed on does not lose it when one person leaves.

> "I am proud not of the parts I made myself, but of the ones my trainees make without mistakes."

## What I pass on first

The habit of measuring rather than assuming. The habit of stopping the line when something is wrong, and not being afraid to. Respect for the next link: the installer on site must receive a part they will not have to struggle with.

## What comes next

The editors will continue the series of stories about people in production. If you have something to tell, write to us.
publications.publications/24/lede: The people, decisions and collaboration that make a project succeed.
publications.publications/24/versions/0/body:
The story of a school project through the eyes of its manager: how the participants agreed on roles, recorded decisions and what helped complete the building without disputes.

## How we started

The project brought together a design office, a general contractor, two subcontractors and the client. At the first meeting we spent a day not on the schedule but on roles: who decides on changes, who is responsible for the model, who for acceptance. It turned out to be the most useful day of the project.

## How we recorded decisions

- One model, one coordinator, one change log.
- Decisions on changes only in writing, with a date and an owner.
- A short weekly report for the client: what was done, what was decided, what awaits a decision.

## Where it was hard

The hardest part was material substitutions: suppliers offered equivalents, and the designers did not have time to check them. A simple rule helped: a substitution is allowed only after the designer's confirmation in the log.

> "The overall result is made not of heroics but of everyone knowing their role and keeping their word in small things."

## How it ended

The building was handed over on time, and acceptance passed without comments on concealed work thanks to staged records. The team continues to work together on the next building.

## What I advise

Start with roles, not with the schedule. Keep one decision log. Agree on substitutions in advance.

publications.publications/25/lede: Which stages to put in the schedule, where weeks are most often lost and how to agree acceptance in advance.
publications.publications/25/versions/0/body:
Façade work often loses weeks not on installation but on waiting for materials and approvals. We look at which stages to build into the schedule and how to agree on acceptance in advance.

## The stages people forget

- Anchor tests on site: without them, subsystem installation cannot start.
- Approval of cladding samples with the client and the architect.
- Delivery of trim pieces: they arrive after the main items and hold up bays.
- Staged acceptance of concealed layers.

## Where weeks are lost

Most often between the delivery of the subsystem and the cladding: the subsystem is installed, and the panels are delayed. Schedule the cladding delivery two weeks ahead of the work front and keep an alternative material in case of a slip.

> "A façade schedule is a delivery schedule. Installation itself rarely breaks the deadline," says a site manager.

## How to agree on acceptance

Agree the report forms and the photo-record procedure before work starts. Define who from the client's side comes to accept concealed layers and within what time after notification.

## A sample schedule

Anchor tests: a week. Subsystem: two weeks per bay. Insulation and wind barrier: a week. Cladding: two weeks. A day for acceptance between stages. In total, one season for an average building with timely deliveries.

publications.publications/26/lede: We trace the chain from plant to site and show which links most often break the deadline.
publications.publications/26/versions/0/body:
Prefabricated structures save time on site but lose it on the road. We trace the chain from the plant to installation and show which links most often break the deadline.

## The supply chain

- Production: the queue at the plant and the readiness of the set, not of individual elements.
- Storage: the plant yard or an intermediate warehouse.
- Transport: oversize loads, permits, travel windows.
- Unloading: crane, laydown area, installation sequence.

## Where days are lost

The most vulnerable link is unloading. The unloading window, the crane queue and the weather affect the deadline more than the distance to the plant. The second weak point is completeness: panels that arrive without embedded parts stand on site for weeks.

> "We thought the main thing was a plant nearby. It turned out the main thing is a free crane on the day the truck arrives," shares a project manager.

## How to plan

Order in sets per installation bay, agree the unloading window with the supplier a week ahead and keep room on site for one extra truck.

## What comes next

The editors are preparing a piece on contract terms for prefabricated deliveries: who pays for truck and crane standing time.

publications.publications/27/lede: Which data about a material the designer, contractor and facility operator need, and how to store it.
publications.publications/27/versions/0/body:
The digital product passport has been discussed for a long time, but in practice it is most often a scan of a paper document. We look at which data designers, contractors and facility managers really need and how to store it.

## Minimum content

- Origin: plant, batch, production date.
- Properties: measured values from the outgoing inspection report.
- Conditions: storage, installation, service.
- Service life and warranty terms.

## Who needs what

The designer needs design properties and confirmation that the system was tested as an assembly. The contractor needs installation and storage conditions. Facility management needs service life and the maintenance and replacement procedure.

> "A passport that cannot be found in five years does not exist. So the main requirement is not the format but the storage," says a head of facility management.

## How to store it

Link the passport to the model element or the specification item, not to the project folder. The batch code on the packaging must lead to the document in one step.

## What gets in the way

The absence of a single format among manufacturers. Until there is one, it is worth demanding at least a machine-readable table of properties together with the paper passport.

publications.publications/28/lede: New methods, transition period deadlines and the questions worth asking a manufacturer now.
publications.publications/28/quiz/0/explanation: Two reports using different methods cannot be compared by the final value.
publications.publications/28/quiz/0/question: What matters more than the final figure in an insulation test report?
publications.publications/28/versions/0/body:
Insulation test requirements are being updated: sampling methods change, scenarios for a humid climate are added, a transition period is introduced. We look at what changes and which questions to ask the manufacturer now.

## New methods

Water absorption and delamination strength tests follow an updated sampling scheme: not from one package but from different points of the batch. This reduces the risk of "showroom" test reports.

- Samples are taken by a laboratory representative, not by the manufacturer.
- The report states the batch number and the sampling scheme.
- A cyclic wetting scenario has been added for façade systems.

## Transition period

Reports under the old method remain valid until the end of the transition period. After that, projects will require new reports, and the laboratory queue is already growing.

> "I advise manufacturers not to wait: laboratories with the right equipment can be counted on one hand," warns a certification expert.

## Questions for the manufacturer

Have the products been tested by the new method? When is it planned? Can we get a report for the batch with the new sampling scheme?

## What it means for projects

Designers should reference the test method in the specification, not only the property values.

publications.publications/29/lede: An industry publication summed up the quarter: demand for subsystems grew, cladding delivery times increased.
publications.publications/29/versions/0/body:
An industry publication has released a review of the façade systems market for the third quarter. According to the review, demand for subsystems grew compared with last year, while cladding lead times increased. The editors give the key figures and market participants' assessments.

## Demand and workload

Subsystem manufacturers report order books two months ahead. The growth is attributed to the completion of large residential projects, the façade season and a shift of some orders from imported systems to local ones. Several companies have announced expansion of production sites.

- The average production time for a subsystem rose from three to five weeks.
- Deliveries of large-format porcelain stoneware are delayed by three weeks on average.
- Aluminium profile prices stabilised after rising in the first half of the year.

## Cladding

The most visible strain is in large-format porcelain stoneware and fibre-cement panels. Suppliers cite limited capacity and the transport queue. Contractors respond with substitutions: some projects switch to metal cassettes and clinker tiles, where lead times are shorter.

> "We revised the schedule of three buildings: the façade goes up later than planned, but we do not keep crews idle. The main thing is that the client learns about the postponement from us, not from the neighbouring site," says a project manager at an installation company.

## What market participants advise

Schedule cladding delivery with a month's margin, fix alternative materials in the contract in case of a slip, and check with the supplier that the batch is in stock before signing the specification.

## What comes next

The fourth-quarter review will be out in January. The editors will prepare an analysis of how market participants are changing supply contracts to fit the new lead times.
publications.publications/30/lede: The façade cladding test method now includes an open-flame scenario; the transition period runs to the end of the year.
publications.publications/30/versions/0/body:
New requirements for fire testing of façade cladding have been approved. The method now includes an open-flame scenario, and the transition period for existing certificates is set until the end of the year. The document concerns panel manufacturers, testing centres and designers.

## What changes in the method

The previous method assessed horizontal flame spread on a façade fragment. The new one adds a vertical scenario: an open-flame source is placed at the base of a specimen at least three metres high, and the assessment is based on the time the flame takes to reach the top edge and on the condition of the insulation behind the cladding.

- The test is run on a full system fragment: cladding, subsystem, insulation and wind barrier.
- The result is tied to the specific combination of materials, not to the panel alone.
- The report must give the temperature in the air gap at three heights.

## Transition period

Certificates issued under the previous method remain valid until the end of the year. After that, using the cladding in projects will require a report under the new scheme. Testing centres warn of a queue: equipment for the vertical scenario is not available everywhere.

> "We booked tests for February even though we applied in October. I advise colleagues not to wait until December," shares a representative of a fibre-cement panel manufacturer.

## What it means for designers

When choosing cladding, check whether the system was tested as a whole in the combination specified in the design. Replacing the insulation or the subsystem without repeat tests formally takes the system outside its certificate.

## What comes next

The regulator promises to publish a list of accredited centres with equipment for the new scenario. The editors will prepare a guide for checking test reports.

The organisers of the construction technology exhibition have announced the programme of the November event in Tashkent. The business part includes thirty sessions on digital design, façade systems and materials logistics. The exhibition runs on 12 to 14 November.

## Programme

The first day is devoted to digital design: model exchange, client requirements and acceptance practice. The second to façades: new test requirements, subsystems and cladding. The third to logistics and procurement: lead times, warehouses, supply contracts.

- Sessions with manufacturers are accompanied by sample demonstrations at the stands.
- A separate area for contractors reviews real details and installation mistakes.
- Young specialists can present projects in the engineering solutions competition.

## Who should come

The organisers target project managers, procurement specialists and technical staff. Registration for industry professionals is free, and the stands can be visited without taking part in the business programme.

> "We deliberately cut the number of talks and increased the time for questions. Last year participants said the most useful things happened in the corridors," explains a representative of the organisers.

## What to prepare

The editors advise drawing up a list of questions for manufacturers in advance and bringing the specifications of current projects: at the stands you can discuss substitutions and lead times with technical specialists.

## What comes next

The editors will work at the exhibition for all three days and publish a summary for each track. Session materials will appear in the events section after the event.

publications.publications/32/lede: The new warehouse will cut dispatch times for sites in the region from two weeks to three days.
publications.publications/32/versions/0/body:
A façade subsystem manufacturer has announced the opening of a new warehouse in the Fergana Valley. According to the press office, the warehouse covers eight thousand square metres, and the shipping time for sites in the region will fall from two weeks to three days.

## What changes for clients

publications.publications/33/lede: A laboratory compared three types of insulation after a year in service in a humid climate.
publications.publications/33/versions/0/body:
A building materials laboratory has published a study on how moisture affects the properties of insulation. Three types of boards were compared after a year of service in a humid climate, and the results were set against laboratory tests.

## How the study was run

Samples of mineral wool, glass wool and expanded polystyrene boards were installed in façade fragments at a test site near Samarkand. After a year, moisture content, thermal conductivity and strength were measured and compared with the initial values.

- Mineral wool boards with a water-repellent treatment showed the greatest stability: the rise in thermal conductivity stayed within the method's error.
- Samples without treatment took up moisture in zones where the wind barrier was faulty.
- Expanded polystyrene kept its properties but showed shrinkage where it was heated by direct sun.

## The main conclusion

The authors stress that the key factor turned out to be not the insulation brand but the quality of the wind barrier installation and the abutments. In zones with properly executed details, all three types kept their declared properties.

> "The difference between a good and a bad detail turned out to be greater than the difference between materials. That is an argument for installation control rather than endless arguments about the choice of insulation," says the head of the study.

## What it means in practice

Designers should detail the wind barrier abutments, and contractors should include a check of these details in the concealed-works reports. Clients should demand photo records before the cladding goes on.

## What comes next

The laboratory will continue monitoring for another two years and widen the sample of manufacturers. The editors will add the study to the collection on choosing insulation.

An architectural glass supplier has launched a tempered façade panel line. The line handles panels up to three metres long, with a capacity of two hundred thousand square metres a year. The first deliveries will go to buildings in Bukhara.

## What the line produces

Tempered and heat-strengthened glass from 6 to 19 millimetres thick, including glass with multilayer coatings. The manufacturer states flatness control after tempering and marking of every panel with a batch code.

- Maximum format: 3000 by 1800 millimetres.
- Insulating glass units can be supplied assembled with a partner plant.
- For façade projects a technologist visits to agree the details.

## Context

Demand for large-format glass for public buildings and industrial halls in the region is growing, while lead times from distant regions reached two months. The local line should cut the time to three or four weeks.

> "For us not only lead times are critical but also the repeatability of tint within a batch. If the line delivers consistency, we are ready to move current projects to it," comments the chief engineer of a design office.

The editors recommend requesting thermal shock and flexural strength test reports for the first batches, and agreeing flatness tolerances in the specification.

publications.publications/37/quiz/0/question: What do concealed-work certificates record under the article's method?
publications.publications/37/versions/0/body:
A rainscreen façade is five layers of which the client ultimately sees one. Everything under the cladding is accepted only during installation: afterwards it can be checked only by opening it up. We split acceptance into five stages and draw up a photo-documented report for each. Here is the whole checklist.

## 1. Brackets

- The spacing and type of brackets match the wind-load calculation for this façade, not a "typical" one.
- Under every bracket a thermal break, an anchor of the brand in the design, embedment depth spot-checked.
- Photos: general view of the wall, close-up of a marked anchor, pull-out test report for the batch.

## 2. Insulation

- Boards fitted tight, no gaps over 2 mm, joints between layers staggered.
- The number of insulation fixings per board as designed, not "as it came out".
- If the insulation got wet before the wind barrier closed it, the stage is not accepted.

## 3. Wind barrier

- Membrane with 100 mm laps, taped, laps running top to bottom.
- Abutments to windows and parapets closed the same day.

## 4. Rails

- Plumb checked on two lines of sight, expansion gap between profiles 8 to 10 mm.
- Stainless steel rivets, no substitution with galvanised ones "from what was available".

## 5. Cladding

- Clips or concealed fixings to the layout plan, joints of equal width.
- Flatness check: deviation no more than 2 mm under a two-metre straightedge.

> The client can request any of the five reports in the project on the platform: we attach them to the stages.

This checklist is neither a secret nor know-how. It is the minimum that lets you understand five years later why a façade holds up or why it does not. If a contractor is not ready to record concealed work, that says more about them than any presentation.

publications.publications/38/lede: Company experience: when a ready kit saves a week and when it costs two reworks on site.
publications.publications/38/versions/0/body:
A ready-made subsystem "in a box" looks convenient: one article number, one invoice, one warranty. In practice we went back to our own assembly, and here is why.

## Where a ready-made kit works

Standard buildings with flat façades and a standard insulation thickness. If the wall has no bays, no reveals deeper than 300 mm and no change of cladding material, a kit saves about a week in procurement and creates no risks.

## Where it breaks down

- Non-standard bracket projections: the kit has two sizes, the building needs four.
- Cladding that changes by floor: porcelain stoneware below, metal above. Different clips, different rail spacing.
- Transitions to curtain walling: the abutment details are almost never in the kit.

Each such case is a separate follow-up order that travels for two weeks while the crew waits.

## What we do

We compile the subsystem specification from the shop drawings of the details, buy profiles and brackets directly from manufacturers and keep a safety stock of standard sizes in the warehouse. It is more expensive in accounting but cheaper in time.

> In the platform catalogue the subsystem is listed as a kit per building, not as a set of article numbers: the price is calculated for the specific façade.

If your building is standard, take the kit and do not overpay. If the façade is complex, ask the contractor how they close the non-standard details. The answer "we will buy more as we go" means crew downtime at your expense.

publications.publications/39/lede: Shisha-Demo on what most often has to be redone in translucent roofs and how to avoid it at the design stage.
publications.publications/39/versions/0/body:
A rooflight is the most capricious glazed structure: snow, water and temperature swings act on it all at once. In three years we have installed fourteen rooflights and met the same mistakes in almost every project.

## Mistake 1. A slope below 15 degrees

Designers love flat rooflights: they look good in renderings. At a slope below 15 degrees water stands on the glazing unit, and the joints last half as long. We propose 20 to 25 degrees or a faceted profile.

## Mistake 2. No snow drift calculation

A rooflight next to a parapet collects snow that the roof as a whole does not have. The load on the glazing unit doubles. The calculation takes a day; replacing glass on site takes a month.

## Mistake 3. Drainage inside the profile not led outside

Condensate collects in the profile, but the channels run into a blank wall. In spring this looks like a leak, although the seals are fine.

> We check all three points at the shop-drawing stage free of charge: it is cheaper than redoing.

We are not designers, but we install what has been designed and we see what lasts and what does not. If you are ordering a rooflight, ask the installer for the list of their typical reworks. Every honest contractor has one.

publications.publications/42/versions/0/body:
## When should fresh concrete be covered in autumn?

As soon as the forecast promises night frosts. Covering and anti-freeze admixtures work together, not instead of each other: the admixture lowers the freezing point of the water, the covering retains the heat of hydration.

## What matters most in a test report?

The test conditions: temperature, humidity, method. Two reports with different methods cannot be compared by the final figure.

## Can a façade be accepted from photographs of concealed work?

Photographs supplement the report, they do not replace it. The parties sign the report; photographs are attached with a date and a reference to the grid line.

## If the drawing and the specification differ, which prevails?

The document the parties expressly named as taking priority in the contract. If there is no such clause, the discrepancy becomes a matter for negotiation, not anyone's automatic fault.

## Who is responsible for a detail that is not in the design?

Whoever invented it on site without approval. Any decision made on the spot must go into the designer's supervision log.

## Does a small building need a digital product passport?

The passport is needed not by the building but by the product: it helps with replacement and repair years later, when the people who built it can no longer be found.
